newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens 96/97 chip profit seen lower.
newsitem.headline: Siemens 96/97 chip profit seen lower.

text.p: German industrial giant Siemens AG, due to offer its semiconductor business outlook on Thursday, was expected to present a picture of solid long-term growth with a few clouds marring the current year.

Battered by declining memory chip prices over the past 15 months, Siemens semiconductor division (HL) is likely to contribute only about 200 million marks ($118.4 million) to group pretax profit this year -- down from 603 million marks in 1995/96, said analysts who follow Siemens.
"Sales are certainly under pressure from worldwide prices," BHF Bank's Juergen Elfers told Reuters. "But I basically have a positive outlook."
Soft prices would dampen HL profit this year, but would not hinder growth over the next five years or so as manufacturers find new uses for microchips, Elfers said.
Sales in the unit, which was Siemens' most profitable last year, should rise above five billion marks, from 4.7 billion marks in the year that ended September 30, the analysts said.
Semiconductor prices began falling about a year ago after several chip makers opened new factories that significantly increased worldwide capacity.

Weaker semiconductor profit was one of the main reasons Siemens forecast no improvement in 1996/97 group profit. In the three-month period ended December 31, group net profit slipped five percent to 478 million marks, while semiconductor sales fell 12 percent to one billion marks.
A spokesman from HL was unavailable for comment on the pretax profit and sales forecasts.

"Long term, HL should see impressive growth, with a rate in the high teens," Elfers said. "The potential is huge" for chips in products like cellular phones, car airbags and credit card-sized smart cards that carry personal, medical and financial data, he said.
Siemens was well positioned to capture some of this new business because it specialises in making ASICs -- chips designed to control specific products like cellular phones, analysts said.
Most of the price declines have come in commodity memory chips called DRAMs.
Since Siemens itself remains HL's largest customer, finding new customers outside remained an important challenge, analysts said.

Elfers said he did not expect HL to follow other Siemens units in presenting ambitious growth plans based on acquisitions. Last month the private telecommunications unit said acquisitions would play a key role in tripling sales over the next ten years.
